questions.topic: Rod inertia about an offset axis
questions.learningObjective: Compute the inertia of a rod about an axis through one end
questions.stem: A 6.0 kg rod of length 2.0 m rotates about a perpendicular axis through one end. What is its moment of inertia in kg m squared?
questions.explanation: A rod about one end has I equals one-third M L squared. One-third times 6.0 times 4.0 equals 8.0 kg m squared.
questions.hint: Use I equals M L squared over three.

questions.topic: A rotation claim that angular momentum forbids
questions.learningObjective: Identify a forbidden rotation outcome
questions.stem: An ice skater pulls in her arms and spins faster. Which claim does conservation of angular momentum forbid?

options.text: Her angular momentum increases without external torque
Her rotational energy stays the same

questions.explanation: With no external torque, angular momentum must stay constant. It cannot increase on its own, so that claim is forbidden.
questions.hint: Check conservation of angular momentum.

questions.topic: Rotational work-energy theorem
questions.learningObjective: Compute work from change in rotational kinetic energy
questions.stem: A wheel's rotational kinetic energy increases from 5 J to 13 J. How much work was done in joules?
questions.explanation: The rotational work-energy theorem says work equals the change in rotational kinetic energy. Thirteen minus five equals eight joules.
questions.hint: Use W equals delta K_rot.

questions.topic: Hoop spun by a tangential force
questions.learningObjective: Compute torque from a tangential force on a hoop
questions.stem: A 0.10 m radius hoop is pushed by a 5.0 N tangential force at its rim. What is the torque in N m?
questions.explanation: Torque equals force times perpendicular distance. Multiplying 5.0 by 0.10 gives 0.50 N m.
questions.hint: Use tau equals F r.

questions.topic: Precession rate versus spin rate
questions.learningObjective: Relate precession rate to spin rate
questions.stem: A top spins at 20 rad/s and precesses at 0.5 rad/s. What is the ratio of spin rate to precession rate?
questions.explanation: The ratio is spin rate divided by precession rate. Dividing 20 by 0.5 gives 40.
questions.hint: Divide the two rates.

questions.topic: Rim acceleration of a driven solid wheel
questions.learningObjective: Compute tangential acceleration at the rim of a solid wheel
questions.stem: A solid wheel of radius 0.40 m has angular acceleration 5.0 rad/s squared. What is the tangential acceleration at the rim in m/s squared?
questions.explanation: Tangential acceleration equals alpha times r. Multiplying 5.0 by 0.40 gives 2.0 m/s squared.
questions.hint: Use a_t equals alpha r.

questions.topic: Disc inertia about a diameter
questions.learningObjective: Compute the inertia of a disc about a diameter
questions.stem: A 4.0 kg disc of radius 0.50 m rotates about a diameter. What is its moment of inertia in kg m squared?
questions.explanation: A disc about a diameter has I equals one-fourth M R squared. One-fourth times 4.0 times 0.25 equals 0.25.
questions.hint: Use I equals M R squared over four.

questions.topic: Angular acceleration from a speed log
questions.learningObjective: Compute angular acceleration from two speed readings
questions.stem: A wheel's angular speed rises from 2.0 rad/s to 8.0 rad/s in 3.0 s. What is its angular acceleration in rad/s squared?
questions.explanation: Angular acceleration equals change in angular speed divided by time. Six divided by three equals 2.0 rad/s squared.
questions.hint: Use alpha equals delta omega over delta t.

questions.topic: Rod inertia about an offset axis
questions.learningObjective: Apply the parallel-axis theorem to a rod
questions.stem: A rod's inertia about its center is I_cm. What is its inertia about a parallel axis a distance d away?
questions.explanation: The parallel-axis theorem adds M d squared to the center-of-mass inertia. The distance must be squared.
questions.hint: Recall I equals I_cm plus M d squared.

questions.topic: A rotation claim that angular momentum forbids
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a skater cannot spin faster without pulling in mass
questions.stem: Why can an ice skater not increase spin rate without changing body shape or applying torque?

answer.exemplar: Because angular momentum is conserved without external torque, so spin rate can only rise if moment of inertia falls.

questions.explanation: Conservation of angular momentum means L stays fixed without torque. Spin rate rises only when inertia decreases.
questions.hint: Link L, I, and omega.

questions.topic: Rotational work-energy theorem
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the rotational work-energy theorem relates
questions.stem: The rotational work-energy theorem relates net work to what quantity?
questions.explanation: The theorem states that net work equals the change in rotational kinetic energy, not angular momentum or displacement.
questions.hint: Work changes kinetic energy.

questions.topic: Hoop spun by a tangential force
questions.learningObjective: Compute angular acceleration of a hoop from a tangential force
questions.stem: A 2.0 kg hoop of radius 0.50 m is pushed by a 4.0 N tangential force at its rim. What is its angular acceleration in rad/s squared?
questions.explanation: Torque is 4.0 times 0.50 equals 2.0 N m. Hoop inertia is M R squared equals 0.5. Alpha equals torque over inertia equals 4.0 rad/s squared.
questions.hint: Compute torque then divide by inertia.

questions.topic: Precession rate versus spin rate
questions.learningObjective: Compute precession rate from torque and spin angular momentum
questions.stem: A gyroscope has spin angular momentum 1.0 kg m squared per second and torque 0.20 N m. What is its precession rate in rad/s?
questions.explanation: Precession rate equals torque divided by spin angular momentum. Dividing 0.20 by 1.0 gives 0.20 rad/s.
questions.hint: Use Omega equals tau over L.

questions.topic: Rim acceleration of a driven solid wheel
questions.learningObjective: Compute total acceleration at the rim
questions.stem: A driven wheel spins at constant angular speed. What acceleration does a rim point have?
questions.explanation: Constant angular speed means zero angular acceleration, so no tangential acceleration. The rim point still has inward centripetal acceleration.
questions.hint: Constant speed means no tangential component.

questions.topic: Disc inertia about a diameter
questions.learningObjective: Explain the inertia of a disc about a diameter
questions.stem: Why is a disc's moment of inertia about a diameter smaller than about its central perpendicular axis?

answer.exemplar: Because mass is distributed closer to a diameter on average, so the squared distances to that axis are smaller.

questions.explanation: About a diameter, much of the mass lies near the axis, reducing the average squared distance compared with the perpendicular central axis.
questions.hint: Compare average squared distances.

questions.topic: Angular acceleration from a speed log
questions.learningObjective: Compute final angular speed from acceleration
questions.stem: A wheel starts at 1.0 rad/s and accelerates at 2.0 rad/s squared for 3.0 s. What is its final angular speed in rad/s?
questions.explanation: Final angular speed equals initial plus alpha times t. One plus 2 times 3 equals 7 rad/s.
questions.hint: Use omega_f equals omega_i plus alpha t.

questions.topic: Rod inertia about an offset axis
questions.learningObjective: Compute inertia of a rod about an offset parallel axis
questions.stem: A 2.0 kg rod has center inertia 0.667 kg m squared. What is its inertia about a parallel axis 0.50 m from the center in kg m squared?
questions.explanation: Apply I equals I_cm plus M d squared. M d squared equals 2.0 times 0.25 equals 0.5. Adding 0.667 gives 1.167.
questions.hint: Add M d squared to center inertia.

questions.topic: A rotation claim that angular momentum forbids
questions.learningObjective: Identify a claim forbidden by angular momentum conservation
questions.stem: A spinning disk on a frictionless axle has no external torque. Which outcome is impossible?
questions.explanation: Without external torque, angular momentum cannot change. A spontaneous doubling violates conservation.
questions.hint: Angular momentum is conserved.

questions.topic: Rotational work-energy theorem
questions.learningObjective: Compute final rotational speed from work
questions.stem: A 2.0 kg m squared inertia wheel receives 16 J of work starting from rest. What is its final angular speed in rad/s?
questions.explanation: Work equals one-half I omega squared. Solving gives omega squared equals 32 over 2 equals 16, so omega equals 4 rad/s.
questions.hint: Solve W equals one-half I omega squared.

questions.topic: Hoop spun by a tangential force
questions.learningObjective: Compute the work done by a tangential force over an angle
questions.stem: A tangential force of 3.0 N acts through 0.40 rad at radius 0.50 m. How much work is done in joules?
questions.explanation: Work equals torque times angular displacement. Torque is 3.0 times 0.50 equals 1.5 N m, and 1.5 times 0.40 equals 0.60 J.
questions.hint: Use W equals tau theta.

questions.topic: Precession rate versus spin rate
questions.learningObjective: Explain why faster spin slows precession
questions.stem: Why does increasing a gyroscope's spin speed decrease its precession rate under the same torque?

answer.exemplar: Because precession rate equals torque divided by spin angular momentum, so larger spin angular momentum reduces the precession rate.

questions.explanation: Precession rate is tau over L. Larger spin speed means larger L, so the rate falls for the same torque.
questions.hint: Inspect Omega equals tau over L.

questions.topic: Rim acceleration of a driven solid wheel
questions.learningObjective: Compute angular acceleration of a solid wheel from torque
questions.stem: A 4.0 kg solid wheel of radius 0.50 m has torque 2.0 N m applied. What is its angular acceleration in rad/s squared?
questions.explanation: Solid wheel inertia is 0.5 M R squared equals 0.5. Alpha equals torque over inertia equals 2.0 over 0.5 equals 4.0 rad/s squared.
questions.hint: Compute I then alpha equals tau over I.

questions.topic: Disc inertia about a diameter
questions.learningObjective: Compute inertia of a disc about a diameter
questions.stem: A 6.0 kg disc of radius 0.30 m rotates about a diameter. What is its moment of inertia in kg m squared?
questions.explanation: Disc diameter inertia is one-fourth M R squared. One-fourth times 6.0 times 0.09 equals 0.135.
questions.hint: Use I equals M R squared over four.

questions.topic: Angular acceleration from a speed log
questions.learningObjective: Compute angular displacement under constant acceleration
questions.stem: A wheel starts at 2.0 rad/s, accelerates at 1.5 rad/s squared for 4.0 s. What is its angular displacement in radians?
questions.explanation: Theta equals omega_i t plus one-half alpha t squared. Two times four plus 0.5 times 1.5 times 16 equals 8 plus 12 equals 20 rad.
questions.hint: Use the constant acceleration displacement formula.

questions.topic: Rod inertia about an offset axis
questions.learningObjective: Compute inertia of a rod about its center
questions.stem: A 3.0 kg rod of length 1.2 m rotates about a perpendicular axis through its center. What is its moment of inertia in kg m squared?
questions.explanation: Rod center inertia is one-twelfth M L squared. One-twelfth times 3.0 times 1.44 equals 0.36.
questions.hint: Use I equals M L squared over twelve.

questions.topic: A rotation claim that angular momentum forbids
questions.learningObjective: Explain why angular momentum cannot change without torque
questions.stem: Why does angular momentum stay constant for a system with no external torque?

answer.exemplar: Because torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, so zero torque means angular momentum does not change.

questions.explanation: Torque equals the time derivative of angular momentum. With zero torque, angular momentum is conserved.
questions.hint: Recall tau equals dL over dt.

questions.topic: Rotational work-energy theorem
questions.learningObjective: Relate torque work to angular displacement
questions.stem: For constant torque, work is computed as torque times what?
questions.explanation: Work by a constant torque equals torque times angular displacement. Power, not work, uses angular speed.
questions.hint: Work is force times distance analog.

questions.topic: Hoop spun by a tangential force
questions.learningObjective: Compute the angular speed after a tangential impulse
questions.stem: A 1.0 kg hoop of radius 0.20 m starts from rest and receives 0.40 N s of tangential impulse at the rim. What is its angular speed in rad/s?
questions.explanation: Angular impulse equals change in angular momentum. Impulse 0.40 at radius 0.20 gives 0.08, inertia is 0.04, so omega equals 2.0 rad/s.
questions.hint: Use angular impulse equals I delta omega.

questions.topic: Precession rate versus spin rate
questions.learningObjective: Compute spin rate from precession rate and ratio
questions.stem: A top precesses at 0.25 rad/s with a spin-to-precession ratio of 80. What is its spin rate in rad/s?
questions.explanation: Spin rate equals ratio times precession rate. Eighty times 0.25 equals 20 rad/s.
questions.hint: Multiply ratio by precession rate.

questions.topic: Rim acceleration of a driven solid wheel
questions.learningObjective: Compute centripetal acceleration at the rim of a driven wheel
questions.stem: A solid wheel of radius 0.60 m spins at 5.0 rad/s. What is the centripetal acceleration at the rim in m/s squared?
questions.explanation: Centripetal acceleration equals omega squared times r. Twenty-five times 0.60 equals 15 m/s squared.
questions.hint: Use a_c equals omega squared r.

questions.topic: Disc inertia about a diameter
questions.learningObjective: Compare disc inertia about diameter and perpendicular axis
questions.stem: For a thin disc, how does inertia about a diameter compare with inertia about the perpendicular central axis?

options.text: Diameter inertia is half the perpendicular inertia

questions.explanation: Perpendicular inertia is one-half M R squared, while diameter inertia is one-fourth M R squared, exactly half.
questions.hint: Compare one-half and one-fourth M R squared.

questions.topic: Angular acceleration from a speed log
questions.learningObjective: Compute angular acceleration from speed log data
questions.stem: What is the angular acceleration in rad/s squared?

options.misconception: uses total speed over total time

questions.explanation: Angular acceleration is change in speed over change in time. From 1.0 to 4.0 in 2 s gives 1.5 rad/s squared.
questions.hint: Use alpha equals delta omega over delta t.

questions.topic: Rod inertia about an offset axis
questions.learningObjective: Compute inertia of a rod about a tangent at its end
questions.stem: A rod of mass M and length L rotates about a perpendicular axis through one end. What is its moment of inertia?
questions.explanation: A rod about one end has I equals one-third M L squared, from the parallel-axis theorem applied to the center inertia.
questions.hint: Use one-third M L squared.

questions.topic: A rotation claim that angular momentum forbids
questions.learningObjective: Explain forbidden spin change
questions.stem: Why can a freely spinning body not change its angular momentum without external torque?

answer.exemplar: Because torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, so zero torque means angular momentum cannot change.

questions.explanation: Torque equals dL over dt. With no external torque, L remains constant.
questions.hint: Recall tau equals dL over dt.

questions.topic: Rotational work-energy theorem
questions.learningObjective: Compute work from rotational speed change
questions.stem: A 3.0 kg m squared inertia wheel speeds from 0 to 4.0 rad/s. How much work is done in joules?
questions.explanation: Work equals change in kinetic energy. Final is 0.5 times 3 times 16 equals 24 J, initial zero, so work is 24 J.
questions.hint: Use W equals delta K_rot.

questions.topic: Hoop spun by a tangential force
questions.learningObjective: Compute angular speed after tangential work
questions.stem: A 1.0 kg hoop of radius 0.50 m receives 2.0 J of work. Starting from rest, what is its angular speed in rad/s?
questions.explanation: Hoop inertia is M R squared equals 0.25. Work equals one-half I omega squared, so omega squared equals 4 over 0.25 equals 16, omega equals 4? Wait 2W/I = 4/0.25=16, sqrt=4. Correct value 4.
questions.hint: Solve W equals one-half I omega squared.

questions.topic: Precession rate versus spin rate
questions.learningObjective: Compute precession rate from torque and L
questions.stem: A gyroscope has spin angular momentum 4.0 and torque 0.80. What is its precession rate?
questions.explanation: Precession rate equals torque divided by angular momentum. 0.80 divided by 4.0 equals 0.20.
questions.hint: Use Omega equals tau over L.

questions.topic: Rim acceleration of a driven solid wheel

questions.explanation: Tangential acceleration equals alpha times r. Six times 0.30 equals 1.8 m/s squared.
questions.hint: Use a_t equals alpha r.

questions.topic: Disc inertia about a diameter

questions.explanation: Disc diameter inertia is one-fourth M R squared. One-fourth times 2.0 times 0.16 equals 0.08.
questions.hint: Use I equals M R squared over four.

questions.topic: Angular acceleration from a speed log
questions.learningObjective: Compute final speed from log
questions.stem: A wheel's speed log shows 3.0 rad/s at t=0 and 9.0 rad/s at t=2.0 s. What is the angular acceleration in rad/s squared?
questions.explanation: Angular acceleration equals change over time. Six divided by 2.0 equals 3.0 rad/s squared.
questions.hint: Use alpha equals delta omega over delta t.

questions.topic: Rod inertia about an offset axis
questions.learningObjective: Explain parallel-axis theorem for rod
questions.stem: Why does a rod's inertia about an end exceed its inertia about the center?

answer.exemplar: Because the end axis is offset from the center of mass, adding M d squared to the center inertia.

questions.explanation: The parallel-axis theorem adds M d squared, where d is L over 2, increasing inertia.
questions.hint: Apply parallel-axis theorem.

questions.topic: A rotation claim that angular momentum forbids
questions.learningObjective: Identify impossible spin outcome
questions.stem: Which outcome is impossible for this body?
questions.explanation: Without external torque, angular momentum must remain constant. Any change violates conservation.
questions.hint: Angular momentum is conserved.

questions.topic: Rotational work-energy theorem
questions.learningObjective: Identify theorem statement
questions.stem: The rotational work-energy theorem states net work equals change in what?
questions.explanation: Net work equals the change in rotational kinetic energy.

questions.topic: Hoop spun by a tangential force
questions.learningObjective: Compute torque from force
questions.stem: A 3.0 N tangential force acts at radius 0.40 m. What is the torque in N m?
questions.explanation: Torque equals force times radius. Three times 0.40 equals 1.2 N m.
questions.hint: Use tau equals F r.

questions.topic: Precession rate versus spin rate
questions.learningObjective: Explain precession dependence on spin
questions.stem: Why does a faster spinning top precess more slowly?

answer.exemplar: Because precession rate equals torque divided by spin angular momentum, so larger spin angular momentum reduces the rate.

questions.explanation: Precession rate is tau over L. Larger spin means larger L, reducing rate.
questions.hint: Inspect Omega equals tau over L.

questions.topic: Rim acceleration of a driven solid wheel
questions.learningObjective: Compute total rim acceleration at constant speed
questions.stem: A solid wheel spins at constant angular speed. A rim point has which acceleration?
questions.explanation: Constant angular speed means zero angular acceleration, so only centripetal acceleration remains.
questions.hint: Constant speed means no tangential component.

questions.topic: Disc inertia about a diameter
questions.learningObjective: Explain disc diameter inertia
questions.stem: Why is a disc's inertia about a diameter half that about its perpendicular axis?

answer.exemplar: Because the mass distribution yields one-fourth M R squared about a diameter versus one-half M R squared about the perpendicular axis.

questions.explanation: Diameter inertia is one-fourth M R squared, perpendicular is one-half M R squared, so diameter is half.
questions.hint: Compare the two formulas.

questions.topic: Angular acceleration from a speed log
questions.learningObjective: Compute angular displacement from log
questions.stem: A wheel starts at 1.0 rad/s, accelerates at 2.0 rad/s squared for 3.0 s. What is its angular displacement in radians?
questions.explanation: Theta equals omega_i t plus one-half alpha t squared. One times three plus one-half times 2 times 9 equals 3 plus 9 equals 12? Wait 0.5*2*9=9, plus 3 =12. Correct value 12.
questions.hint: Use theta equals omega_i t plus one-half alpha t squared.

questions.topic: Rod inertia about an offset axis
questions.learningObjective: Compute inertia of rod about offset
questions.stem: A 4.0 kg rod has center inertia 0.533 kg m squared. What is its inertia about a parallel axis 0.60 m from center?
questions.explanation: M d squared equals 4.0 times 0.36 equals 1.44. Adding 0.533 gives 1.973.
questions.hint: Add M d squared.

questions.topic: A rotation claim that angular momentum forbids
questions.learningObjective: Explain conservation
questions.stem: Why is angular momentum conserved in an isolated system?

answer.exemplar: Because no external torque acts, and torque is the rate of change of angular momentum.

questions.explanation: In an isolated system external torque is zero, so angular momentum does not change.
questions.hint: Zero torque means conserved L.

questions.topic: Rotational work-energy theorem

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg m squared inertia wheel speeds from 1.0 to 5.0 rad/s. How much work in joules?
questions.explanation: Initial KE is 0.5 times 2 times 1 equals 1 J. Final is 0.5 times 2 times 25 equals 25 J. Difference 24 J.
questions.hint: Use W equals delta K_rot.

questions.learningObjective: Explain tangential force effect
questions.stem: Why does a tangential force at the rim produce angular acceleration?

questions.explanation: A tangential force at radius r produces torque tau equals F r, which drives angular acceleration.
